summary: Summation No. 12 covers September 1946 in American-occupied South Korea. The month was dominated by the railroad strike of 22 September, which spread to postal, telegraph, newspaper and Seoul City Hall workers, halted transport of grain and supplies, and produced a food crisis; General Hodge's 27 September address blamed radical agitators. Military Government announced on 13 September that Korean directors would take full charge of departments, with Americans advisory, and new Civil Service classification rules took effect 30 September. Other items include the Child Labor Ordinance (No. 112), arrest orders for three Communist Party leaders, suspension of three leftist newspapers, an attempt on Syngman Rhee's life, rising cholera (14,614 cases), the opening of Seoul National University, barter trade with Japan, rationing figures, price indexes and Bank of Chosen note circulation. The report is rich in statistical charts and tables useful to economic and social historians.
highlights: On 22 September more than 30,000 railroad workers struck without prior mediation, halting all rail transport in South Korea; on 27 September General Hodge blamed agitators and urged a return to work and negotiation with the National Labor Mediation Board.

The strike spread to postal, telegraph, newspaper and Seoul City Hall workers, halting grain and supply transport and deepening a food crisis in which 6,500,000 depended on rations and only 88,650 metric tons of summer grain were collected.

On 13 September the Military Governor declared that Korean directors must take full charge of departments with Americans only advisory; Rules Number 3 of 30 September set up a civil service classification and pay system.

Arrest of Communist Party leaders Pak Heun Young, Lee Kang Kook and Lee Chu Ha was ordered but not carried out; three leftist newspapers were suspended, two Chung Ang editors were sentenced to 18 months, and an attempt was made on Syngman Rhee's life on 12 September.
Rations were 270 grams daily in Seoul and 250 elsewhere, summer grain collection reached 52 percent of the pre-flood estimate, and black-market rice hit 43 yen per pound in Seoul.
Cholera reached 14,614 cases and 9,474 deaths by 30 September, worst in Kyongsang-namdo (1,549 cases); repatriation continued, with 812,559 Japanese and 915,500 Koreans repatriated to date.

Child Labor Ordinance No. 112, effective 14 September, barred industrial work by children 14 and under, with maximum hours effective 15 February 1947; government barter with Japan began, shipping 24,000,000 yen of graphite, fluorite, talc and fish for coal and industrial goods.

Seoul National University opened with 6,799 students registered by 21 September despite opposition; schools adopted a 6-6 structure, 4,225,000 textbooks were distributed, and Bank of Chosen notes reached 11,341,307,000 yen.

sections.title: Front matter
sections.summary: Library covers and stamps, title page for No. 12 (September 1946), contents of four parts, and a list of 37 charts, graphs and maps.

sections.title: Part I: General
sections.summary: Digest of the month: Koreans take over departments, the 22 September rail strike, the Rhee assassination attempt, grain collection shortfalls, the new Women's Bureau and rising cholera.

sections.title: Section 1. Political Activities
sections.summary: The Military Governor announced Korean control of departments on 13 September; new civil service classification followed. Hodge addressed the strike on 27 September; Communist arrest orders and the attempt on Rhee also noted.

sections.title: Section 2. Economic Activities
sections.summary: Strikes cut coal and mail service and a Seoul Public Utilities Board was formed. Barter shipments to Japan reached 24,000,000 yen; a food crisis developed and Bank of Chosen notes stood at 11,341,307,000 yen.

sections.title: Section 3. Social Activities
sections.summary: Women's Bureau created; 278,905 repatriation spaces; cholera rising; 6,799 students at Seoul National University; new 6-6 school system; three newspapers suspended.

sections.title: Part II: Political
sections.summary: Government and politics, including Hodge's statements and party activity, followed by legal developments, crime, police, prisons, and the constabulary and Coast Guard.

sections.title: Section 1. Government and Politics
sections.summary: Legislature planning, Korean directors taking charge, civil service academy and pay rules, Hodge's statements on unity and the rail strike, party conventions, and 75 registered national organizations.

sections.title: Administration and Civil Service
sections.summary: Legislature preparations; the 13 September policy of Korean control; a Civil Service Training Academy with 120 students; and the Rules Number 3 compensation plan.

sections.title: Political Affairs
sections.summary: Hodge spoke on unity, the 8 September anniversary and the rail strike. Rhee's society held a convention; Communist arrest orders issued; Hong Jin died; 75 national organizations registered.

sections.title: Interzone Activities, Joint Commission and Foreign Affairs
sections.summary: No North-South mail in September and a growing refugee flow. American delegates stood ready to reopen the Joint Commission; reactions to the Wallace address and a Chinese repatriation list.

sections.title: Section 2. Legal and Public Safety
sections.summary: New revenue stamps, child labor trials, press convictions, the 12 September attempt on Rhee, police graduations, crime charts, prisons holding 17,049 inmates, and the constabulary and Coast Guard.

sections.title: Part III: Economic
sections.summary: Natural resources (crops, fisheries, coal, minerals) and commerce and industry: production, transport, communications, labor, Japan trade, rationing, prices and finance.

sections.title: Section 1. Natural Resources
sections.summary: Rice and grain collections, the Sung Duk project, fisheries output and China exports, fuel wood needs, August coal output of 26,516 tons, and mineral and smelter problems.

sections.title: Agriculture
sections.summary: Grain collections were hampered by profiteering and the strike. Sung Duk project 80 percent complete; 700 orchards bonded; Land Development Company dissolved; 175,408 cho of mulberry.

sections.title: Fisheries
sections.summary: Production of 3,601 tons in July and 968 in August, 44,700 kg exported to China, agar-agar capacity, 33,227 sail boats, and cloth allocated for sails.

sections.title: Forestry and Mining
sections.summary: Winter fuel wood estimated at 150,000 pyong for Seoul; coal output 26,516 tons; mineral needs, Changhang smelter, Onjin and Ilkwan mines; gold mining prohibited.

sections.title: Section 2. Commerce and Industry
sections.summary: Industry, rail and road transport, postal and telegraph services, strikes and labor law, Japan trade, food rationing and price indexes, and currency and finance.

sections.title: Industry
sections.summary: Technical and material shortages persisted. Paper production peaked but the Hokusen newsprint mill at Kunsan faced shutdown; railway additions cost 717,000 yen; flour mills resumed.

sections.title: Transportation and Public Utilities
sections.summary: Travel restrictions lifted 30 September; the rail strike stopped all trains from 22 September; 17 of 33 lighthouses operating; Kyonggi Trucking Service and the Seoul Public Utilities Board.

sections.title: Communications
sections.summary: Post office strikes at Taegu, Kyongju and Seoul; a fourth mail shipment of 287 pieces to the U.S.; money order figures; Cheju-do cable repair; radio owners up to 180,342.

sections.title: Labor
sections.summary: Strikes by 30,000 railroad workers, telegraph and City Hall staff; Child Labor Law effective 14 September; 42,265 union members in 239 unions; employment and wage tables.

sections.title: Imports and Exports
sections.summary: Barter with Japan sent out 24,000,000 yen of graphite, fluorite, talc and fish; coal (511,504 tons January-September), locomotives, textiles and chemicals came in.

sections.title: Rationing and Price Control
sections.summary: 6,500,000 on rations; 88,650 tons of summer grain collected; 270-gram Seoul ration; black-market rice at 43 yen; price indexes, controlled commodity distribution and Food Regulation No. 3.

sections.title: Finance
sections.summary: Bank of Chosen notes at 11,341,307,000 yen, rising loans and deposits, gold prices, and licensing of Tai Han Life Insurance Company with 10,000,000 yen capital.

sections.title: Part IV: Social
sections.summary: Public health and welfare, education, culture and religion, and public information, followed by the map of Korea and blank or library end pages.

sections.title: Section 1. Public Health and Welfare
sections.summary: Women's Bureau, repatriation totals, refugee camps with 27,657 people, medical college recognition, nursing and veterinary transfers, supply shipments, vaccine stocks, and cholera at 14,614 cases.

sections.title: Public Welfare and Repatriation
sections.summary: Welfare training institutes, Women's Bureau duties, Yonghori Leprosarium with 600 patients, 812,559 Japanese and 915,500 Koreans repatriated, and 27,657 North Korean refugees.

sections.title: Medical, Nursing, Pharmaceutical and Veterinary Affairs
sections.summary: 2,906 physicians renewed licenses; five medical colleges recognized; child mortality of 180 per thousand in the first year; Pusan nursing institute; veterinary work transferred to Koreans.

sections.title: Supply
sections.summary: Final 20,000,000 yen Civil Affairs Division medical allocation, 1,000,000 vitamin pills, 300 tons of UNRRA clothing at Inchon, and biological production tables for vaccines.

sections.title: Preventive Medicine
sections.summary: Water plant survey, DDT spraying at Pusan, cholera at 14,614 cases and 9,474 deaths, communicable disease charts, and a typhus campaign begun in Seoul on 16 September.

sections.title: Section 2. Education, Culture and Religion
sections.summary: Seoul National University opened with 6,799 students; 6-6 school system and core curriculums; 4,225,000 textbooks; Chu-suk festival; 4-H vote in Kyonggi-do; missionary returns.

sections.title: Education
sections.summary: Seoul National University registration and opposition, teacher resignations, school construction shortages, the new 6-6 structure, core curriculum tables and textbook distribution.

sections.title: Culture, Athletics and Religion
sections.summary: Chu-suk festival on 10 September; 4-H vote with 229,367 households in favor; Girl Scout leader school at Ewha; Olympic planning committee; 22 returned missionaries.

sections.title: Section 3. Public Information
sections.summary: Campaigns on the Child Labor Ordinance and rice collection, film releases, the new Culture Hour radio program, suspension of three leftist newspapers, and press comment on food and political unity.

sections.title: Information Programs, Motion Pictures and Radio
sections.summary: Child labor publicity, a black-market campaign, the Labor Information Party in Chungchong-namdo, eleven films released, and Culture Hour and Workers' Song broadcasts.

sections.title: Press and Public Opinion
sections.summary: The Military Governor's 17 September free press statement, suspension of Chosun In Min-Po and two others, and press comment on the legislature, food, Wallace's resignation and Korean takeover.

sections.title: Map of Korea and end pages
sections.summary: Map of Korea on page 97, followed by blank scans, a library due-date card and the back cover.
